extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy; lawmakers and theorists interested in origins and justification of civil government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative principles Locke gives about the formation, ends, and limits of family, conjugal, and political societies — including consent, majority rule, purpose of government, and limits on absolute power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ends of marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: The ends of marriage are procreation and mutual support and assistance whilst the spouses are together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil magistrate does not abridge the natural rights necessary to those ends but only decides controversies between man and wife about them. Nothing unnecessary to the ends of marriage (procreation and upbringing until children can provide for themselves) should be imposed as essential to the conjugal condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and determinability of conjugal bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugal bonds need not necessarily be perpetual for life; they may be made determinable by consent, for a certain time, or upon certain conditions, as other voluntary compacts can be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no positive law requires perpetuity, marriage contracts may be limited or conditional; this is consistent with the natural purposes of marriage so long as procreation and education are secured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of husband's authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the man naturally has the final determination in matters of common interest as the abler and stronger, his power reaches only to things of common interest and property; the wife retains full possession of her peculiar rights and the husband has no more power over her life than she has over his.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The husband's authority is not absolute; the wife has liberties (including, in many cases, liberty to separate) where natural right or contract allows. Conjugal society's arrangements may vary by contract or custom but must not assume absolute dominion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between servant and slave
rubrics_metrics.description: A freeman becomes a servant by selling his service for a time in exchange for wages (temporary, contract-limited power), whereas a slave, captured in a just war, is subjected to absolute dominion and arbitrary power and, having forfeited his life and liberties, cannot be considered part of civil society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Servitude is contractual and limited; slavery (as Locke describes it) implies loss of capacity for property and exclusion from civil society. This distinction grounds different legal/political treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family is not a political commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a family may resemble a little commonwealth in order and offices, it is very far from a political society in constitution, power, and end; the paterfamilias' power is distinct and limited as to time and extent over different persons in the household.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A master's domestic authority does not equate to legislative power over a people; limits include lack of general legislative power of life and death except in the special case of slaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of political society (consent to quit natural power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political/civil society exists only where every member has quit his natural executive power to punish breaches of the law of nature and has resigned it to the community, creating standing rules and an impartial judicature to decide controversies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essential marker of political society is the relinquishment of private judgment/executive power and acceptance of a public authority (laws and judges) to preserve property and adjudicate disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of civil society is the preservation of property — that is, life, liberty, and estate — as far as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All powers of the commonwealth (laws, punishments, war and peace) are oriented toward protecting members' property. If government fails in this, it undermines the very reason for its establishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of legislative and executive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative and executive powers originate where the community (having received authority from individuals joining it) sets laws and appoints those to execute them; members thereby owe assistance to execute those judgments when called.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislature determines punishments and laws for internal offences; executive power determines responses to external injuries — both draw authority from the consent of the people comprising the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule as necessary for a body politic to act
rubrics_metrics.description: When individuals consent to make one community, that community is one body which must act by the will/determination of the majority; the act of the majority is received as the act of the whole to enable the body to move and continue as one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without majority binding the whole, a community cannot function as a single political body. Therefore, those who join a commonwealth are understood to give up powers necessary to its ends to the majority, unless a greater number was expressly agreed upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective legislature to prevent arbitrary exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislature placed in collective bodies (senate, parliament, etc.) prevents single-person exemption from laws and guards property by making laws as the act of the whole body politic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective legislative authority restricts usurpation by any one individual and ensures that every person, equally, is subject to laws they helped establish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompatibility of absolute monarchy with civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute monarchy, where one man holds both legislative and executive power without any impartial judge or appeal, is inconsistent with civil society because subjects have no earthly judge to appeal to and thus remain, in relation to the prince, in the state of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no appeal exists against the ruler, subjects suffer the worst inconveniences of the state of nature and lose the security civil society is meant to provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of appeal and equal subjection to the law
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil society requires that every member have an appeal to law and judges for decision of controversies and redress of injuries; no man in civil society can be exempted from its laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principal use of public power is to give laws to all under it; obedience is required unless the law of reason or God necessarily enjoins the contrary. Exemption of any person undermines civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of commonwealth by consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of any lawful government is the consent of a number of freemen capable of a majority to unite and incorporate into one body politic; this compact is the sole thing that constitutes a political society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent to unite is sufficient to form a commonwealth; explicit historical instances may vary, but the theoretical foundation rests on voluntary agreement to join for mutual preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reasons for early preference for monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Early societies commonly chose monarchy because it was simple, familiar (paternal precedent), suited to small populations, and effective for defense and war, where singular command is practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for single rulers in early polities is explained as pragmatic (defense, familiarity, simplicity), not as proof of natural paternal or monarchical right; as societies grow, other forms and restraints may become necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of rulers based on consent and fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: When several families or peoples unite, they will (by their natural freedom) choose as ruler the person they judge ablest, fittest, or most likely to rule well; paternal pre-eminence may explain beginnings but not legitimate indefinite domination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership arises from consent and perceived fitness (age, wisdom, courage); tradition and custom may favour heirs, but consent remains the legitimating source.
